It steps a small grid on the render thread every frame (well under a millisecond); Intensity is how much heat is fed in. Fireworks Fireworks over the host: a rocket climbs from the bottom edge and bursts into a sphere of streaking sparks that slow, fall, crackle and fade. Fire(Point?) sends one to a point (or a spot of its own), FireOnPress fires where you press, and Interval keeps a show going. Shots overlap. Light adds on dark surfaces, color shows on light ones. FlutedGlass Reeded glass over what is behind the host: parallel convex ribs, each a cylindrical lens that shows a squeezed, flipped strip of the backdrop, with a color split toward its edges, a sheen and a shaded groove. Fog Banks of mist drifting across the shape at DriftSpeed, thickest at the bottom and thinning out toward Height. Over the content it hangs in front of it; under a see-through panel it is a background. Under reduced motion it holds still. Frost Ice that creeps in from the shape's edges in feathery crystal branches, frosting what is under it (the content, for an Over layer): blurred, whitened toward Tint, with glints. Amount is how far it has crept in; animate it with a transition to freeze or thaw. It melts in a ragged circle around the pointer and freezes back when the pointer leaves. Genie Hides the content by pulling it into a point, like a window minimizing into the dock, and pours it back out to show it. The sides bend in toward the point first, then the content slides down the funnel into it. The point is the center of Target (a dock icon, a button), the point given to Hide(Point?) or Show(Point?), or the bottom center of the content. The content is captured and hidden while it plays, and handed back once shown. Under reduced motion it fades. The funnel draws outside the host on its way to the point, so it is cut by any clipping ancestor between the content and the target. Glass A pane of liquid glass over what is behind the host: a beveled rim that refracts and splits the backdrop, a little magnification, an optional frost, a specular rim facing the light and a soft drop shadow. It reads what is drawn behind it, so it follows anything that moves there. Glitch A digital glitch over the content: bands of it tear sideways, blocks jump, the color channels split, a few rows flash in the glitch colors and scanlines show. It changes in steps (about 20 a second), as a broken signal does. It draws nothing between glitches, so a burst layer costs nothing until it fires: a short burst on Trigger() or a press (an error, a denied action), or, with IsContinuous, now and then on its own. Under reduced motion a burst is a short, mild color split and a continuous glitch stays still. Glow Bloom around the shape. The light is a tight Gaussian plus a wide one through a soft knee, so a tinted glow keeps its hue instead of clipping to white. Switching IsLit off cools the light (it shrinks, deepens and dims) instead of cutting it. Grain Film grain inside the shape, per device pixel. Static by default, so it never shimmers. GrainGradient A linear, radial or conic gradient whose colors scatter into film grain: triangular noise scatters the ramp position, so colors stipple into each other, plus brightness grain. Halftone Print-style round dots on a rotated screen, sized by a tone; neighboring dots merge where the tone is dark. HeatHaze Shimmering hot air: what is behind wobbles in rising, turbulent noise. By default it rises above the shape, strongest a little up the column (pair it with Fire); with WholeShape it fills the shape. HoloFoil Holographic foil over the shape: an iridescent rainbow sheen whose bands shift as the pointer moves over it, fine etched lines, glitter that flares as the angle passes each facet, and a soft glare under the pointer. Still when the pointer is away (unless it drifts), so idle it costs nothing. Ink Colored ink in a fluid over the content: moving the pointer pushes the fluid and leaves ink in a color that changes as it goes, a press throws a splash of every color, and the ink swirls, spreads and fades. A small fluid simulation runs on the render thread only while there is ink; with none it draws nothing and costs nothing. Under reduced motion the ink stays where it lands and fades. InnerShadow Light and shade inside the child's own shape, its text or icons: a pressed-in (inset), raised (emboss) or letterpress look, lit from LightAngle. It follows the shape exactly (from the distance to its edge, which the host measures when it captures the child), so it works on glyphs, not just boxes. After changing something deep inside the child, call RefreshMask(). Jelly Pressed, the element squashes and wobbles like jelly before it settles: a damped spring that squashes it down and out, then overshoots, plus a bulge that spreads from the press point. While it wobbles the layer draws a capture of the content (the real content is hidden and still takes input), and hands back to it once settled. Under reduced motion the wobble is a small, quick squash. LightLeaks Warm film light leaking in over the shape's edges: four long, soft glows that drift along the frame and breathe in and out, whitening where they are hottest. Added as light over the content (a photo, a hero card); over light content it draws as tinted haze. LightRays Shafts of light falling across the shape from a source just outside it, like sun through a window: a fan of rays that shimmer and shift slowly, bright where they come in and fading with distance. Added light, as tinted haze on a light surface. Under reduced motion the rays hold still. LiquidMetal A polished metal slab reflecting a photo studio: a rolled rim, a domed face and a flowing, domain-warped surface, with conductor Fresnel and optional thin-film color. As a border it is a round tube. LiquidProgress A liquid filling the shape to Level: for progress bars, gauges and battery or storage levels. The surface waves, bubbles rise, and a change of level eases in with a little overshoot and sloshes the surface. Bind Level to a progress value (0..1). Magnifier A glass loupe that follows the pointer over the host and magnifies what is under it: the content and what is behind it. It grows in when the pointer arrives and fades when it leaves; PointAt(Point?) aims it from code (a tour, keyboard focus). MeshGradient Up to six colors pinned to points that drift slowly, blended smoothly in OKLab (so blends never go muddy) with Shepard weights: each color owns its point, blends fall off smoothly. Metaballs Glossy blobs that drift on slow paths and merge, over a base color. Each blob takes one of the colors in turn. MotionBlur A smear of the content along its motion, behind it, while the host moves: a slide-in, a drag, a fling, a transform animation. It reads how the host moves in its window every frame, so any movement counts (scrolling too). Still, it draws nothing. The host captures the content when it changes; call RefreshMask() after changing something deep inside it. OldFilm What is behind it as an old print running through a projector: toned toward sepia, darker at the corners and grained, weaving a little in the gate and flickering at 18 frames a second, with scratches that run down it for a few frames and specks of dust that come and go. Under reduced motion it holds one frame. Outline A stroke around the child's own shape, its text, icons or a cut-out picture, at an exact width whatever the shape (from the distance to its edge, which the host measures when it captures the child). Sticker adds a soft shadow under a thick border. Outside strokes go under the child, centered ones over it. After changing something deep inside the child, call RefreshMask(). PagePeel Hovered, a corner of the element curls up like a sticker or a page and shows its back, with a shadow under the curl; it peels further as the pointer nears the corner and settles back when the pointer leaves. IsPeeled holds it peeled from code. While peeled the layer draws a capture of the content (the real content is hidden and still takes input). ParticleNetwork Dots drifting across the shape, joined by fine lines whenever two come close: the closer, the stronger the line. The pointer joins in as one more point that draws the nearby dots toward it. Drawn with Skia directly; each dot's path is a function of time, so a given time always draws the same frame. Under reduced motion the dots hold still. Plastic A plastic slab under one soft light: a diffuse base that keeps its color, a GGX highlight widened by the light's size, and a faint sky at grazing angles. Still, so it costs nothing per frame once drawn. PointerShadow The pointer is a light over the page and the content casts a soft shadow away from it, in the shape of the content's own pixels: further and softer the further the light is, up to MaxOffset. Within PointerReach of the content the light follows the pointer across the whole window, so every card on a page casts its shadow away from it; beyond that, or with no pointer, the light rests above the content and the shadow falls just below it. ProgressiveBlur What is behind the shape goes from sharp to fully blurred toward one Edge: a header or a tab bar over a scrolling list, where content fades into the bar instead of meeting a hard line. The ramp crossfades five copies of the backdrop (sharp, then blurred by an eighth, a quarter, a half and all of Blur), so every point sees a real blur, not a mix of sharp and blurred. Tint fades toward the bar's own color. Pulse Rings and halos that follow the shape's outline, tap ripples, and pings that fly to a destination. RainGlass Rain on a misted pane over what is under it: beads that come and go, fine droplets, and drops that slide down in fits and starts, leaving a clear wet trail dotted with droplets. Each drop is a small lens showing what is behind it upside down. Fog mists the glass between them. Under reduced motion the drops hold still. RetroGrid A synthwave floor: glowing grid lines running toward a horizon under a gradient sky, with a striped sun. For hero sections and splash screens; as a fill it paints the shape under the child. Reveal Shows or hides the host's content with a dissolve, a burn, a pixelate, an iris, a wipe, a melt, a clock wipe, a grid of diamonds, a swirl, halftone dots, or noise resolving into it. Set IsShown (or call Show(Point?) and Hide(Point?)): the layer captures the content as it looks, hides the real element and plays the transition on the capture, then hands back to the element. While hidden the element is invisible but keeps its place in the layout. With nothing to capture yet (invisible, or not laid out) it switches at once. Under reduced motion it fades. Shatter Breaks the content into glass shards that fly apart and fall, or turns it to dust that blows away (hide), and brings it back together (show): for delete, dismiss and undo. Set IsShown, or call Hide(Point?) and Show(Point?) with the point the break starts from. Shards are cut around that point, smaller near it; dust leaves from that point outward or, with no point, from the side the wind blows toward. The pieces are drawn with Skia directly from a capture of the content, which is hidden while they fly. Under reduced motion it is a short fade. Shimmer A sheen band sweeping across the shape: skeleton loaders and "Thinking…" surfaces. The band starts and ends off the shape, so it never cuts. Under reduced motion the surface breathes. Shockwave A one-shot ring of compressed air that bends what is behind it as it spreads from a point, with a color split at the front, a highlight where there is content to catch it, and a faint rim so it still reads over a plain backdrop. Shots overlap. Silk A background of soft satin folds that flow slowly: a few warped folds lit by one soft light, shading into their creases with a broad sheen along the ridges. For hero sections, sign-in pages and cards; as a fill it paints the shape under the child. Sparkles Crisp four-point stars around the shape, each with its own size (mostly small, a few large), twinkle rate and spin. Continuous stars rest between appearances so only a few are lit at once. Burst() pops every star once and flings it out a little. Spoiler Hides the host's content until it is revealed, as messaging apps hide spoilers: shimmering dust over a heavy blur, a mosaic, or a solid cover. A tap opens it in a soft circle from the tap point; IsRevealed binds both ways, and HideAfter covers it again. Wrap a TextBlock (or any element) in an FXHost with this layer. Spotlight A soft light that follows the pointer across the shape and lights the border nearest to it, fading in when the pointer arrives and out when it leaves. It also reacts to a pointer just outside the shape (within PointerReach), so the border lights up as the pointer approaches. Idle, it draws nothing and costs nothing. Starfield A night sky: twinkling stars in three depths, shooting stars, or warp streaks. Swirl Colors stirred into a slow swirl: a twist around the center over twice domain-warped noise, through the color ramp (blended in OKLab). Tilt The host leans toward the pointer in 3D and grows a little, and a glare slides across it with the pointer, like a card turned under a light. The lean is a perspective render transform on the host, so the host's other layers (a glow, a shadow) lean with it; it eases on every frame while it moves and is removed once the host settles flat. While it leans it takes the place of a render transform set on the host itself. Under reduced motion the host stays flat and only the glare follows the pointer. Topography The contour lines of a slowly changing landscape, like a topographic map: thin lines of even width wherever the slope is, every fifth one bolder. A calm background for a hero or an empty state. Under reduced motion it holds still. Trail A trail behind the pointer as it moves over the host: a glowing ribbon or a stream of sparks, head color to tail color. A still pointer leaves nothing, so idle it costs nothing; under reduced motion there is no trail. VoiceOrb A living orb of color for voice input: three soft lights drift inside a glassy sphere, their colors meeting smoothly, with a glow around it. Bind Level to the microphone level: the orb swells, its edge rolls and the lights drift faster as it rises. Level changes are eased (quick to rise, slower to fall), so a raw meter reading looks smooth. VoiceWave Glowing waves across the shape that swell with the voice: three colors crossing each other under an envelope that pinches them to nothing at the ends, lying almost flat and drifting slowly when quiet. Bind Level to the microphone level; changes are eased (quick to rise, slower to fall), and the waves drift faster as it rises, without jumping. Pairs with VoiceOrb. Voronoi Cells around seed points that orbit slowly, with exact seams and cells shaded toward their rim. Each cell takes one of the colors. Water The content under a sheet of water: moving the pointer over it drags ripples across the surface, a press drops a splash, and Rain lets drops fall on their own. The waves bend what is under them and catch the light. A small wave simulation runs on the render thread only while the water moves; calm water draws nothing and costs nothing. Waves Layered bands of color, one per color from back to front, with rolling, swaying crests; each front band shades the one behind it. Weather Rain streaks or snowflakes falling in three depths, slanted by the wind, over the shape. Structs FXDrawStats Totals for one layer type since the last reset. Enums BeamStyle BokehPreset ColorFilterPreset ConfettiShape ConfettiStyle DitherPattern DitherPreset ElectricStyle FXAnchor Where a fill's pattern is pinned. FXBlendMode How a layer composites onto what is beneath it. FXCorner A corner of the shape, in Avalonia's order (as Avalonia.CornerRadius). FXEdge A side of the shape. FXPlacement Where a layer draws relative to the host's child. FXSurface What a host sits on, for light layers (glows, pulses, sparkles, lightning). FXToneInput What a re-toning fill (dither, halftone) reads as its tone. FireStyle FlutedGlassPreset GlowStyle GradientKind GrainGradientPreset InnerShadowStyle LiquidMetalPreset MeshGradientPreset MetaballsPreset OutlinePosition OutlineStyle PlasticPreset PulseStyle RevealStyle ShatterStyle SilkPreset SpoilerStyle StarfieldStyle SwirlPreset TrailStyle VoronoiPreset WavesPreset WeatherStyle

docs/concepts/content-masks.html.title: Content masks | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/content-masks.html.summary: Content masks Most layers follow the child's shape: its bounding box with rounded corners. Some follow the child's own pixels instead: the letters of a text, the outline of an icon, the colors of a picture. For those, the host captures the child into a mask. Layers that follow the content Layer What it takes from the content Glow with Style="Mask" Blooms around the child's own pixels (text, icons) instead of its box. Shimmer with UseMask Sweeps across the child's own pixels: "Thinking…" text. Every fill with UseMask Paints only the child's own pixels: gradient or aurora text, a liquid-metal logo, holographic icons. ColorFilter with UseMask Recolors only the child's own pixels: an icon, not the card around it. Outline Strokes the child's own shape at an exact width, or cuts it out as a sticker. InnerShadow Shades the inside of the child's own shape: inset, emboss or letterpress. AmbientGlow Blurs the child's own colors and spreads them behind it. MotionBlur Smears a capture of the child along its motion. PointerShadow Casts a shadow in the shape of the child's own pixels. The fills are the gradients, materials, patterns and backgrounds: liquid metal, plastic, holo foil, silk, mesh gradient, grain gradient, swirl, waves, voronoi, metaballs, dither, halftone, fluted glass, liquid progress, retro grid, starfield, dot grid, weather, caustics, bokeh, code rain and beams. With UseMask a fill goes over the child, unless its Placement says otherwise. Examples Gradient text: <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:MeshGradient UseMask="True" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <TextBlock Text="Aurora" FontSize="46" FontWeight="Black" /> </fx:FXHost> A glow around the letters of a label, not its box: <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Glow Style="Mask" Color="#f472b6" Radius="10" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <TextBlock Text="LIVE" FontSize="32" FontWeight="Bold" Foreground="White" /> </fx:FXHost> A "Thinking…" shimmer that sweeps across the text only: <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Shimmer UseMask="True" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <TextBlock Text="Thinking…" FontSize="16" /> </fx:FXHost> A sticker cut out around a picture: <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Outline Style="Sticker" Color="White" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Image Source="/Assets/logo.png" Width="96" /> </fx:FXHost> When the host captures The host captures its child on the UI thread, by rendering it to a bitmap, and builds six halving, slightly blurred levels from it on the CPU, once per change. The capture extends past the child by as far as the layers reach (a mask glow's radius), up to 128 DIPs. Layers that need color (the ambient glow, motion blur) keep the child's colors as well as its coverage. The host captures again when: the child's size or the display scaling changes; one of the child's own properties changes; the child is replaced; a layer is added that needs more than the last capture had (color, a distance field or a wider reach). Properties that can't change the child's pixels by themselves are ignored: pointer-over, focus, DataContext, Tag, Name, Transitions, Cursor, the context menu and flyout, Focusable, IsHitTestVisible and tooltips. A style those trigger, such as a background on pointer-over, changes real properties, and those count. The host only watches the child itself, not its descendants. After changing something deeper inside the child, call RefreshMask: // StatusText is a TextBlock inside the StackPanel that is the host's child. StatusText.Text = "Uploaded"; StatusHost.RefreshMask(); While changes keep coming, captures are spaced about 100 ms apart, with one more once they stop. For the ambient glow behind a video, call RefreshMask() as the frames change. The distance field Outline and InnerShadow need to know how far each pixel is from the edge of the child's own shape, on both sides, at an exact distance whatever the shape. The mask's blurred levels can't tell them that, so when one of these layers is in the host, the capture also builds a distance field: an exact Euclidean distance transform of the child's coverage, once to the nearest inside pixel and once to the nearest outside one. The field stores one byte a pixel, in steps of a quarter of a DIP, from 16 DIPs inside the edge to 47.75 DIPs outside it. That range bounds how far an outline or an inner shadow can reach. A pixel counts as inside when its alpha is at least half the child's own strongest alpha, so text in a translucent color, or a child at Opacity 0.4, still has a shape. Cost A capture happens on the UI thread, and only when something changed; nothing is captured per frame. The distance field is the costly part. It takes a few milliseconds for a card on the desktop: about 4 ms for a 340×190 card with extra padding at 2× scaling, 2.4 ms with an ordinary pad, and 13 ms for a 700×500 panel. In the browser without ahead-of-time compilation the card takes about 14 ms, and text about 2 ms. While the child keeps changing, the host reuses the last field and builds a new one once the changes settle. Limits Only the child itself is watched. Call RefreshMask() after changing something inside it. Very large content gets a softer mask. A capture is limited to 4096 pixels on a side and 8 million pixels (4 million with a distance field). A larger child is captured at a lower scale. A failed capture doesn't throw. If the child can't be captured (out of memory, a texture too large for the platform, a child that fails to render), the host logs a warning and the layers that need the mask draw nothing. The transitions use their own capture. Reveal, Genie, Shatter, Jelly and PagePeel capture the content once, as it looks when they start, and hide the real element while they stand in for it. See One-shots and the pointer.

docs/concepts/layers.html.title: Layers and hosts | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/layers.html.summary: Layers and hosts Every effect in Nova.Avalonia.FX is a layer, and every layer lives in a host. This page covers how the two work together. The host FXHost is a control that takes one child (its Child, the XAML content) and draws a list of layers around it (its Layers). It keeps two drawing surfaces: one under the child and one over it. <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="16"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Glow Color="#7c5cff" Radius="18" /> <fx:Grain Amount="0.08" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="240" Height="120" Background="#15171c" /> </fx:FXHost> The layers follow the child's shape: its bounds and corner radius. The corner radius comes from FXHost.CornerRadius when it is set, or else from the child itself when it is a Border or a templated control. The shape uses one radius for every corner (the top-left one). Set CornerRadius="999" for a capsule or a circle. Light that spills past the child (a glow, a pulse, flames) is drawn outside the host's bounds, so any clipping ancestor cuts it: a ScrollViewer, a Border with ClipToBounds, or Fluent's ContentControl, which clips by default. Leave room around the host inside such containers, or set ClipToBounds="False" where that is safe. A layer draws with its host, so a later sibling covers anything the layer draws past the host. Give the host a higher ZIndex when, for example, a ping should land on top of another control. A layer can be in one host at a time. Adding a layer that is still in another host's Layers throws an InvalidOperationException: remove it from the first host, or give each host its own layer. How layers stack Each layer draws either under the child or over it. Its Placement decides which: Placement Where the layer draws Auto (the default) The layer's own default: light that spills out goes under, overlays go over. Under Behind the child, like a background or a glow. Over On top of the child, like a sheen or grain. With Auto, glows, the pulse's rings, fills, glass and backgrounds go under the child; the shimmer, grain, sparkles, lightning, ripples, distortions, transitions and the pointer layers go over it. A fill with UseMask goes over the child, since it paints the child's own pixels (see Content masks). Within each placement, layers paint in the order they appear in Layers: the first one is painted first, and each later one on top of it. <fx:FXHost.Layers> <!-- Under the child: the glow first, then the fill on top of it. --> <fx:Glow Color="#22d3ee" /> <fx:MeshGradient Preset="Lagoon" /> <!-- Over the child, the shimmer's own default. --> <fx:Shimmer /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> Blend modes BlendMode sets how a layer composites onto what is beneath it: Blend mode Effect Normal (the default) Premultiplied source-over. Screen Light that brightens without ever exceeding white. Plus Additive light. Multiply Darkens by the layer's color. Overlay Multiplies or screens, depending on what is beneath. SoftLight A gentler overlay. Light layers already draw as light over a dark surface. For pure additive light, set BlendMode="Plus" or "Screen". A transparent caustics layer with BlendMode="Screen", for example, lights the content under it: <fx:Caustics WaterColor="Transparent" BlendMode="Screen" Placement="Over" /> Properties every layer has Every layer derives from FXLayer and has these properties: Intensity is the strength of light on light layers (aurora, electric, fire, glow, grain, light leaks, light rays, pulse, shimmer and sparkles), up to 3; the coverage of fills, up to 1; and a dimmer that fades every other layer. So a transition on Intensity fades any layer in and out. Opacity fades the layer, from 0 to 1. Speed multiplies the layer's clock, from 0 to 4. Changing it never makes the animation jump, and at 0 the layer stops. A layer's own pace settings (a FlowSpeed, Drift, FallSpeed and the like) run on that clock and don't make it jump either: the pattern carries on from where it is. The show and hide transitions run on their Duration instead. Seed picks the random layout of layers with randomness (noise, scattered stars, confetti). Two layers with different seeds look different; the same seed always draws the same frames. Placement and BlendMode, described above. IsActive switches the layer off: it draws nothing, costs nothing, and ignores presses and the pointer. RenderScale shades the layer at a fraction of the display's resolution (0.25 to 1) and scales it up. It is meant for large, soft, heavy layers; see Performance. Layers drawn as shapes (confetti, fireworks, shatter, particle network) don't use it. Each layer also reports ReadsBackdrop, which is true for layers that read what is drawn behind the host (see below). Property Type Default Description Intensity double 1 How strong the layer is. Light and fills read it as their own strength (a glow's brightness, up to 3; a fill's coverage); on other layers it is a dimmer that fades the layer, like Opacity. 0 draws nothing. Range 0–3. Opacity double 1 How opaque the whole layer is: 0 invisible, 1 as drawn. Range 0–1 (0–100%). Speed double 1 Multiplies the layer's clock. Changing it never makes the animation jump. Range 0–4. Seed int 1 Picks a variation of the layer's random pattern (its noise, where pieces fall); the same seed always draws the same picture. Layers without randomness ignore it. Range 1–999. Placement FXPlacement Auto Where the layer draws: behind the host's child, over it, or (Auto) where the layer usually goes. Values: Auto, Under, Over. BlendMode FXBlendMode Normal How the layer combines with what is beneath it: painted over it (Normal), or blended as light or color. Values: Normal, Screen, Plus, Multiply, Overlay, SoftLight. IsActive bool true Whether the layer draws. Off, it draws nothing, costs nothing and ignores the pointer and presses; a transition layer then shows or hides its content at once. RenderScale double 1 Shades at this fraction of the display's resolution and scales the result up: 0.5 shades a quarter of the pixels. For large, soft layers (a window-sized aurora or swirl), where the cost grows with the area; edges and grain soften. 1 (the default) is full resolution. Range 0.25–1 (25–100%). Not every setting applies to every layer, or to every style of a layer: Seed and Speed only matter on layers with randomness or motion, and many settings belong to some styles only. The gallery's settings panel shows only the settings that do something, from what FXCatalog knows. Idle layers cost nothing A layer asks the compositor for frames only while it moves. A layer at rest draws once and then asks for nothing: still layers, such as a plastic fill, a static grain or a glow that doesn't breathe; layers that are switched off, or at an Intensity or Opacity of 0; one-shot layers between shots: a glitch draws nothing until it fires; pointer layers while the pointer is away: a spotlight draws nothing and costs nothing until the pointer arrives; the small simulations (simulated fire, ink, water) once they have settled or emptied; every layer of a host that is hidden, or scrolled out of view. When you change a setting, only that layer is snapshotted again, and the host sends at most one update per frame. Layers that read the backdrop Some layers show or change what is drawn behind them: glass, fluted glass, the magnifier, progressive blur, frost, rain on glass, water, heat haze, shockwave, CRT, chroma split, glitch, old film, ASCII, the color filter, the spoiler (except its Solid style), and dither or halftone with Input="Backdrop". Their ReadsBackdrop is true. Such a layer copies its region of the window's surface just before it draws. Glass and FlutedGlass sit under the child, so they bend what is behind the host; the distortions sit over it, so they bend the child too. Inside an offscreen layer (an ancestor with Opacity below 1, an effect, or a clip that needs a layer), the copy can't see that ancestor's content. Keep such ancestors opaque. Styles, bindings and presets Layers are styled elements. They join the host's logical tree, so they inherit its DataContext, and styles, bindings, dynamic resources and transitions apply to them like to any other property: <fx:FXHost Classes="hover"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Glow Color="{DynamicResource SystemAccentColor}" IsLit="{Binding IsOnline}" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="200" Height="80" CornerRadius="12" Background="#101217" /> </fx:FXHost> <Style Selector="fx|FXHost.hover fx|Glow"> <Setter Property="Intensity" Value="0.2" /> <Setter Property="Transitions"> <Transitions> <DoubleTransition Property="Intensity" Duration="0:0:0.3" /> </Transitions> </Setter> </Style> <Style Selector="fx|FXHost.hover:pointerover fx|Glow"> <Setter Property="Intensity" Value="1.3" /> </Style> Many layers have a Preset or a Style that sets several values at once. Presets apply at template priority: a local value, or a style with a class or pseudo-class, wins over a preset; a plain type-selector style does not. Fills painted from a list of colors (mesh gradient, swirl, waves, grain gradient, voronoi, metaballs, dither and bokeh) take up to six colors in Colors. Unset, they use the preset's palette. In XAML, separate the colors with commas, semicolons or spaces; hex values, color names and CSS forms such as rgb(43, 27, 90) all work: <fx:MeshGradient Colors="#2b1b5a, #ff6f91, #ffc46b" /> The catalog FXCatalog describes every layer type: its id, display name, summary and parameters, with their ranges, units, choices and the styles they apply to. The gallery builds its navigation and settings panel from it. ToXaml writes a layer back as XAML, as its preset or style plus the values that differ: using Nova.Avalonia.FX; using Nova.Avalonia.FX.Catalog; foreach (var info in FXCatalog.Layers) Console.WriteLine($"{info.Id}: {info.Name}, {info.Parameters.Count} settings"); var glow = new Glow { Style = GlowStyle.Neon, Radius = 20 }; Console.WriteLine(FXCatalog.ToXaml(glow)); // <fx:Glow Style="Neon" Radius="20" />

docs/concepts/light-and-dark.html.title: Light and dark surfaces | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/light-and-dark.html.summary: Light and dark surfaces Light layers such as a glow, a pulse, sparkles or lightning add light, as rune draws them. That reads well on a dark surface. On a light surface, added light would vanish into white, so these layers know which surface they sit on and change how they draw. How light layers draw on each surface On a dark surface, light adds to what is beneath it: rings, halos and stars brighten the background, and the hottest parts turn white. On a light surface, glow, pulse, sparkles and lightning draw as tinted haze instead: saturated color, white-hot cores in the layer's own color, and faint light kept faint, so a radar's rings stay rings instead of merging into a wash. Lightning's core becomes a crisp line in a deep shade of the color over a pale tint of its glow. A white light, such as the spotlight's default, stays white. Very pale colors still read weakly on white, so pick deeper colors for light themes. Other layers adjust to the surface in their own way: Layer On a light surface On a dark surface Fire Simulated flames draw as color over the smoke; the procedural smoke veil and dim tips stay fainter. Flames add light. Fireworks The sparks show as color. The sparks add light. Holo foil Pastel bands. A thin film's cooler colors, added as light. Frost The crystal lines darken a little, where white ice alone would vanish. White ice. Halftone The dots leave a margin of paper at the edge, so the outline still shows. Inner shadow An inset adds a faint lip of light along its far edges. Liquid progress The wave behind the surface is paler and see-through. Pointer shadow A deeper shadow. Reveal A dissolve's edge catches a faint light. Shatter The shards' edges are dark. Voice orb Its glassy rim is fainter. The layers that know the surface are ambient glow, beam, border beam, electric, fire, fireworks, frost, glow, halftone, holo foil, ink, inner shadow, light leaks, light rays, liquid progress, pointer shadow, pulse, reveal, shatter, sparkles, spotlight, trail, voice orb and voice wave. The other layers draw the same on both. How the host picks its surface FXHost.Surface sets the surface for every layer in the host: Surface Meaning Auto (the default) Follows the host's theme: a light theme is a light surface, a dark theme a dark one. Dark Light adds, as rune draws it. Light Light shows as tinted haze, so it neither vanishes into white nor washes it out. With Auto, the host reads its actual theme variant, so it follows the application's theme, a ThemeVariantScope around it, or a theme switch while the app runs. FXHost.IsLightSurface tells you which surface the host is using now. Set the surface yourself when the theme doesn't describe what is behind the layers, for example a dark card in a light app: <fx:FXHost Surface="Dark"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Pulse Style="Radar" Color="#22d3ee" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="64" Height="64" CornerRadius="32" Background="#101217" /> </fx:FXHost> You can also put the card in a ThemeVariantScope with RequestedThemeVariant="Dark"; the host then picks the dark surface on its own, and so do the card's own theme resources. Theme the colors Layer colors are ordinary Color properties, so they can come from theme resources. Define a color per theme and use it with DynamicResource; the layer changes color when the theme changes: <Application.Resources> <ResourceDictionary> <ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries> <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Light"> <Color x:Key="StatusGlowColor">#0e7490</Color> </ResourceDictionary> <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Dark"> <Color x:Key="StatusGlowColor">#22d3ee</Color> </ResourceDictionary> </ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries> </ResourceDictionary> </Application.Resources> <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="999"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Pulse Style="Radar" Color="{DynamicResource StatusGlowColor}" /> <fx:Glow Color="{DynamicResource StatusGlowColor}" Radius="9" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Ellipse Width="14" Height="14" Fill="#16a34a" /> </fx:FXHost> A few tips: Fire reads best on dark UI. For pure additive light on any surface, set BlendMode="Plus" or "Screen". See Blend modes. Most fills, glass layers and backgrounds draw the same on both surfaces: give them colors that suit each theme, as above.

docs/concepts/one-shots-and-pointer.html.title: One-shots and the pointer | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/one-shots-and-pointer.html.summary: One-shots and the pointer Most layers run on their own. Some play a moment when asked (a ripple, a burst, a zap), some show and hide the content with a transition, and some follow the pointer. This page covers all three. One-shots A one-shot plays once and then draws nothing, so it costs nothing until it fires. Shots overlap: firing again while one is still playing starts another one beside it, so a quick double tap shows two ripples. Each layer keeps a bounded pool of live shots. When it is full, the pulse, the shockwave, the electric zaps and the sparkle bursts fade their oldest shot out; the other layers drop it. Ink and water add each splash to their simulation instead. Layer From code On a press Notes Pulse, Ripple style Trigger(at) TriggerOnPress (on) A ripple from a point, confined to the shape. Pulse, Ping style Ping(to), PingTo(control) TriggerOnPress (on) A ping flies from the shape's edge to a point or a control. Interval sends one every so many seconds. Sparkles Burst() BurstOnPress (off) Pops every star once. With IsContinuous off, stars only show during a burst. Electric Zap(at) ZapOnPress (off) One strike. On an arc, a zap at a point strikes from the nearer node to it. Shockwave Trigger(at) TriggerOnPress (on) A ring that bends what is behind it. Glitch Trigger() TriggerOnPress (on) A short burst over the whole content. With IsContinuous it glitches now and then on its own instead. Confetti Fire(at) FireOnPress (off) A burst from a point, or the style's own origin. Fireworks Fire(at) FireOnPress (off) A rocket that bursts at a point. Interval keeps a show going. Ink Splash(at) SplashOnPress (on) A splash of every color. Water Splash(at) SplashOnPress (on) A splash on the water's surface. DotGrid Ripple(at) RippleOnPress (on) A ring sent out across the grid. Jelly Wobble(at) WobbleOnPress (on) The element squashes and wobbles. Beam Send() Sends one pulse along the path. Pulses also leave every Interval seconds. The point is in the host's coordinates. Leave it out (or pass null) to use the center of the shape or the layer's own spot. A press on the host passes the press point, except for a ping, which flies along its Direction. To fire at a point from an event, convert the position to the host: private void OnCardReleased(object? sender, PointerReleasedEventArgs e) { CardRipple.Trigger(e.GetPosition(CardHost)); } To send a ping from one control to another, give the sending host a higher ZIndex so the ping lands on top of the target: <fx:FXHost ZIndex="1"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Pulse x:Name="Pinger" Style="Ping" TriggerOnPress="False" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Button Content="Send" Click="OnSend" /> </fx:FXHost> <Button x:Name="Inbox" Content="Inbox" /> private void OnSend(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) { Pinger.PingTo(Inbox); } Show and hide transitions Reveal, Genie and Shatter show and hide the host's content. Set IsShown, which binds both ways by default, or call Show(from) and Hide(toward). When a transition starts, the layer captures the content as it looks, hides the real element and plays the transition on the capture. Once the content is shown again, the element takes over in the same frame as the layer stops drawing. While hidden, the element is invisible but keeps its place in the layout. With nothing to capture (no content, invisible, or not laid out yet), or while the layer isn't active, it switches at once. Duration sets the pace in seconds; the layer's Speed doesn't apply. <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Reveal x:Name="DetailsReveal" Style="Iris" IsShown="{Binding IsDetailsVisible}" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="260" Height="140" CornerRadius="12" Background="#15171c" /> </fx:FXHost> The point given to Show or Hide is where the transition comes from or goes: an iris opens there or closes on it, shards break from it and fly back toward it, the genie pours out of it or pulls into it. private void OnDismiss(object? sender, PointerReleasedEventArgs e) { DetailsReveal.Hide(e.GetPosition(DetailsHost)); } Genie can also pull the content into another control, such as a dock icon or a trash button, with Target: <fx:Genie Target="{Binding #TrashButton}" Duration="0.6" /> Other layers that change state with a short animation: Spoiler hides content until it is tapped. IsRevealed binds both ways, Reveal(from) and Hide() work from code, and HideAfter covers it again after so many seconds. PagePeel curls a corner up when hovered; IsPeeled holds it peeled from code. LiquidProgress eases to a new Level with a little overshoot and sloshes its surface. Glow cools over Cool seconds when IsLit turns off. Frost creeps in as far as Amount; animate it with a transition to freeze or thaw. Layers that follow the pointer These layers react to the pointer moving over the host: Layer What follows the pointer From code Reach Spotlight A soft light that lights the border near it. PointAt(at) PointerReach, 48 DIPs past the shape by default HoloFoil The sheen shifts as if the foil tilted. PointAt(at) The shape Magnifier A glass loupe. PointAt(at) The shape Trail A ribbon or sparks behind the pointer. PointAt(at) PointerReach, 0 by default Ink The pointer stirs the fluid and leaves ink. PointAt(at) The shape Water The pointer drags ripples across the surface. Splash(at) The shape Frost The ice melts around the pointer. PointAt(at) The shape, while MeltRadius is above 0 DotGrid Dots light up and grow around the pointer. PointAt(at) HoverRadius, 90 DIPs by default ParticleNetwork The pointer joins in and draws the dots toward it. PointAt(at) The shape, while FollowPointer is on Tilt The host leans toward the pointer, with a glare. PointAt(at) PointerReach, 0 by default PointerShadow The content casts a shadow away from the pointer. PointAt(at) PointerReach, 800 DIPs by default, while FollowPointer is on PagePeel The corner peels further as the pointer nears it. IsPeeled The shape, while FollowPointer is on The host listens to the window's pointer only while one of its layers follows it and is active. It passes the pointer's position to a layer while the pointer is within the shape plus the layer's reach, and tells the layer once the pointer leaves. On the render thread, the layer eases toward the pointer and fades in and out; where a layer has FollowTime, that is how long it takes to catch up. Idle, these layers draw nothing. PointAt(at) aims a layer from code, as if the pointer were there: for keyboard focus, a guided tour or a demo. Pass null to let it go. The pointer takes over again when it moves. This lights a card's spotlight on its button when the button gets keyboard focus: SaveButton.GotFocus += (_, _) => { var center = new Point(SaveButton.Bounds.Width / 2, SaveButton.Bounds.Height / 2); CardSpotlight.PointAt(SaveButton.TranslatePoint(center, CardHost)); }; SaveButton.LostFocus += (_, _) => CardSpotlight.PointAt(null);

docs/concepts/performance.html.title: Performance | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/performance.html.summary: Performance The layers are built to cost little and to cost nothing at rest. This page lists what they cost, the settings that change it, and how to measure it in your own app. What a layer costs The numbers below were measured with the gallery's --bench on an Apple M4 Max (Metal, Retina 2×). Each layer sits on a 340×190 card over a moving scene, so it redraws every frame. GPU times leave out the fixed cost of waiting for the GPU, which only the benchmark pays. Idle: nothing. A layer that isn't moving requests no frames. CPU (render thread): 2–50 µs per layer per frame; progressive blur costs the most. A few layers do per-frame work of their own before they draw: electric 0.06 ms, aurora 0.08 ms, ink's fluid 0.22 ms and the simulated fire 0.39 ms. First frame of an effect: 2–10 ms, which includes compiling its shader (see Warm up the shaders). When the system's shader cache doesn't hold the effect's GPU pipeline, it takes 20–60 ms, at times up to about 200. GPU time per frame on the card: GPU time Layers Under 0.1 ms Nearly half the layers, including glow, shimmer, outline, inner shadow, jelly, tilt and the voice orb. 0.1–0.2 ms Pulse, reveal and its melt, mesh gradient, aurora, starfield, CRT, chroma split, glitch, color filter, light leaks, water, old film, sparkles, trail and heat haze. Ambient glow, motion blur and pointer shadow cover 0.75–1 Mpx and still take 0.14–0.16 ms. 0.2–0.3 ms Glass, fire, fog, shockwave, voronoi, and ASCII, plus a blurred copy of what is behind. 0.3–0.45 ms Swirl, liquid metal, spoiler, topography (it takes the height three times a pixel for the slope), caustics and bokeh. Over 0.5 ms Rain on glass 0.51 ms; frost 0.62 ms; progressive blur 1.0 ms, the most, for its five copies of what is behind. Progressive blur and frost don't animate, so they only redraw when what is behind them changes. A few layers are drawn as Skia shapes instead of a shader, so their cost is on the CPU, with almost no GPU time. That time swings up to four times from run to run: fireworks 0.04–0.18 ms, confetti 0.1–0.5 ms, the particle network 0.09–0.32 ms, shatter's shards 0.1–0.4 ms while they fly, and shatter's dust 0.13–0.6 ms while it blows. Slower GPUs scale these numbers up, but the ranking holds. Cost grows with the area A layer's GPU cost grows with the area it shades. A 700×500 panel of swirl takes about 0.77 ms per frame. Layers only shade where they can draw. Flames and heat haze cover the area above the shape, not around it; a shockwave covers only its live rings; layers that only draw around the pointer repaint only around it; and the border-only layers (the border beam and the electric border) skip the interior. Layers that read the backdrop copy only the margin they sample. Render scale RenderScale shades a layer at a fraction of the display's resolution and scales the result up. At 0.5 it shades a quarter of the pixels: <fx:Swirl Preset="Marble" RenderScale="0.5" /> On a 700×500 panel, RenderScale="0.5" takes: Layer Full resolution RenderScale="0.5" Swirl 0.77 ms 0.56 ms Liquid metal 0.73 ms 0.47 ms Voronoi 0.76 ms 0.40 ms Aurora 0.62 ms 0.28 ms Use it for large, soft, heavy layers, such as a window-sized aurora or swirl. Edges and grain soften. On cheap layers it costs more than it saves, because the scale-up pass takes about 0.1 ms: grain went from about 0.07 ms to 0.10–0.19 ms. Layers drawn as shapes (confetti, fireworks, shatter, particle network) don't use it. Warm up the shaders The first frame of an effect waits for its shader to compile. FXSettings.WarmUpAsync compiles every shader up front, in about 60 ms on the machine above. Start it early, for example when the app starts: public override void OnFrameworkInitializationCompleted() { // Set up the main window or view here. _ = FXSettings.WarmUpAsync(); base.OnFrameworkInitializationCompleted(); } On the desktop the shaders compile in parallel on the thread pool, off the UI and render threads. In the browser there is one thread, so they compile one at a time, and the task yields to the browser between them so input and rendering go on; each compile still holds the UI thread for its own few milliseconds. The warm-up compiles the shaders but not the GPU pipelines, which are built on each effect's first draw. The system caches those from one launch to the next. On the first launch on a machine, or once the system has dropped them from its cache, an effect's first frame takes 20–60 ms, at times up to about 200. Content masks Layers that follow the content's own pixels capture the child on the UI thread when it changes, not per frame. The distance field that Outline and InnerShadow need costs a few milliseconds per capture on the desktop. Content masks has the numbers. In the browser The browser runs .NET on one thread, so the app, the compositor and the effects share it, and the GPU work goes through WebGL. The shaders run as fast as on the desktop. What costs more is .NET code, which the browser interprets unless the app is compiled ahead of time (RunAOTCompilation). Measured with ?bench on published builds, in Chrome on the Apple M4 Max at 60 Hz: Interpreted Compiled ahead of time As it is All 70 at 59–60 fps All 70 at 59–60 fps CPU 4× slower (a mid-range laptop) All 70 at 58–60 fps; the simulated fire 44 All 70 at 57–60 fps Download (Brotli) 5.9 MB 9.4 MB In Safari 27 on the same machine (interpreted; Safari can't slow the CPU down), 64 of the 66 ran at 59–60 fps in a full run; the other two, shatter's shards (56) and fireworks (52), hold 60 when timed on their own. Safari compiles all the shaders in 67 ms. The effects added since (the color filter, dot grid, outline, inner shadow, beam, the five newer reveals, ink, silk and beams) all hold 60 fps there too, with 0.03–0.28 ms of .NET work a frame. The layers that do their work in .NET code are the ones that slow down: Layer Interpreted Compiled ahead of time Shatter's dust 0.9–1.1 ms a frame 0.25–0.5 ms Electric's bolts 0.45–0.6 ms 0.12–0.3 ms Simulated fire 0.4–0.45 ms, plus 1.4–1.5 ms for its simulation steps 0.18–0.4 ms, plus 0.35–0.8 ms Compiled ahead of time, these timings swing about two times from run to run. If your app leans on the simulated fire, shatter's dust or electric and has to run well on slower machines, compile it ahead of time. Otherwise the interpreted build is enough. The browser gallery compiles ahead of time on a Release publish, with these properties in its project: <PropertyGroup> <RunAOTCompilation Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Release'">true</RunAOTCompilation> <WasmDebugLevel Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Release'">0</WasmDebugLevel> </PropertyGroup> WasmDebugLevel 0 turns off debugger support in Release. With debugger support on, the runtime also stops optimizing interpreted code: shatter's dust took 6.6 ms a frame and ran at 22 fps even on the M4 Max. WebGL can't make Skia wait for the GPU, so there is no GPU time in the browser: the frame rate is the measure. Measure in your own app FXDiagnostics times draws per layer type in your own app. It is off by default and free while off. Turn on IsEnabled, and MeasureGpu for GPU times, then read Collect(): FXDiagnostics.IsEnabled = true; FXDiagnostics.MeasureGpu = true; // waits for the GPU on every draw: for measuring only // Later, after the screen you want to measure has run for a few seconds: foreach (var stats in FXDiagnostics.Collect()) { Console.WriteLine( $"{stats.Layer}: {stats.Draws} draws, {stats.CpuMsPerDraw:0.000} ms CPU, " + $"{stats.GpuMsPerDraw:0.000} ms GPU, {stats.MegapixelsPerDraw:0.00} Mpx a draw"); } MeasureGpu makes every draw wait for the GPU, which slows frames down: use it to compare layers, not in a shipping app. FXDiagnostics.Backend tells you which GPU backend the measured draws ran on. The gallery's bench The desktop gallery times every layer in a real window on the GPU the app uses: dotnet run -c Release --project samples/Nova.Avalonia.FX.Gallery.Desktop -- --bench bench.csv Add --target 6 for the full-stage panel, --set RenderScale=0.5, --only fire,swirl (or a style, --only shatter:Dust), --full-quads to measure without trimming, or --cold to skip the warm-up. Besides every layer, a full run times shatter's dust, reveal's melt and the simulated fire on their own. bench/baseline.csv is a full run on the machine above. To see whether a change made anything slower, run the bench again on the same machine and compare: dotnet run -c Release --project samples/Nova.Avalonia.FX.Gallery.Desktop -- --bench bench/run.csv --compare bench/baseline.csv It lists the layers that got slower or faster by more than run-to-run noise (25% and 0.04 ms on the GPU, 50% and 0.02 ms on the CPU), and exits with 1 when any got slower. A layer that looks slower is timed again first, up to twice, and keeps its best run: GPU clocks change with load, and the CPU time of the layers drawn as shapes swings up to four times from run to run. Timings only compare on the same machine and setup (the first line of the CSV records it). After a deliberate change, copy the new run over the baseline. Close other busy apps while it runs. First frames read 20–200 ms in a run where the system's shader cache didn't hold the layers' pipelines, and 2–10 ms in the run after; the compare leaves them out. The bench keeps its window on top while it runs and ignores the real pointer, which would take over from the scripted one. It exits with 2 when layers ran far under the frame rate of the others or drew nothing, as when the window was covered, on another desktop, or the display slept: their timings don't compare, so run it again. Timing in the browser ?bench times every effect in the browser gallery (?bench=glow,fire:Simulated for some, &seconds=3 each): the frames painted a second, the 95th-percentile frame time and each draw's CPU time, printed in the console. A page in a hidden tab or window paints a frame a second or none, so scripts/browser-bench.mjs runs it in a headless Chrome, which also lets it slow the CPU down. It needs Node 22 or later and Chrome: node scripts/browser-bench.mjs # against the gallery on http://localhost:5240 node scripts/browser-bench.mjs --cpu 4 # with the CPU 4 times slower node scripts/browser-bench.mjs --url http://localhost:8080/ --only electric,shatter:Dust node scripts/browser-bench.mjs --verify # ?verify instead node scripts/browser-bench.mjs --safari # in Safari (a new tab; keep it in view) Not measured yet: Firefox, phones, and slower GPUs.

docs/concepts/reduced-motion.html.title: Reduced motion | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/concepts/reduced-motion.html.summary: Reduced motion Every layer has a reduced-motion pose: a calm version of the effect with no travel. One switch turns it on for the whole app. Turn it on Set FXSettings.ReducedMotion: using Nova.Avalonia.FX; FXSettings.ReducedMotion = true; Every host updates its layers before the next frame. The setting can change at any time, from any thread; the hosts rebuild their layers on the UI thread. Avalonia doesn't report a system reduced-motion preference, so the app decides. Set it from your app's own setting, for example a switch on a settings page: <ToggleSwitch x:Name="ReduceMotionSwitch" Content="Reduce motion" IsCheckedChanged="OnReduceMotionChanged" /> private void OnReduceMotionChanged(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) { FXSettings.ReducedMotion = ReduceMotionSwitch.IsChecked == true; } The poses Under reduced motion, layers keep their look but stop traveling: Layers Reduced-motion pose Glow and other lights Lights still cool when switched off: a fade, not travel. Pulse The rings become a static halo. Fills: gradients, materials, patterns and backgrounds Each holds one fixed pose. Shimmer The surface breathes instead of sweeping. Aurora, grain, light leaks, light rays, fog, topography, particle network, rain on glass, border beam They hold still. Beam A still gradient along the path. Old film It holds one frame. Voice orb, voice wave The colors and waves hold still; they still swell with Level. Fire The flames hold one pose and the embers stop; the simulated styles hold their current state. Electric The continuous bolt holds one shape; a zap still strikes. Reveal, Genie, Shatter A short fade, at most a quarter of a second. Spoiler It switches at once. Confetti, fireworks The pieces appear in place and fade, without flying. Glitch A burst is a short, mild color split; a continuous glitch stays still. Jelly A small, quick squash. Page peel A quick peel. Tilt The host stays flat; only the glare follows the pointer. Trail No trail: it only exists as motion. Motion blur No smear: the host still moves, but nothing is drawn behind it. Ink The ink stays where it lands and fades. Water Gentler ripples and splashes, and no rain. Liquid progress The level jumps, and the surface stays calm. Dot grid The lit dots jump to the pointer, and presses send no ripples. Spotlight, magnifier and other pointer layers They jump to the pointer instead of easing, and appear and fade at once. A transition's length is decided when it starts, so switching reduced motion halfway through doesn't put it out of step. Check the poses In the gallery, the settings flyout switches motion between full and reduced. The desktop gallery also renders the poses headless: dotnet run --project samples/Nova.Avalonia.FX.Gallery.Desktop -- --snap reduced.png --reduced --effect glow Fixed time Separately from reduced motion, FXSettings.Clock replaces the compositor clock for every layer, in seconds. Every frame is a pure function of time, so the same time always draws the same frame. Use it for deterministic snapshots and for stepping through an effect: FXSettings.Clock = () => 2.3; // every layer draws as it looks 2.3 s in FXSettings.Clock = null; // back to the compositor clock

docs/effects/ambientglow.html.title: Ambient glow | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/effects/ambientglow.html.summary: Ambient glow Ambient glow lights the space behind the host's child with the child's own colors, like a screen's ambient light on the wall behind it. The host captures the child's pixels in color, and the layer blurs them, spreads them out from the center and draws them under the child. Use it behind album art, a video frame, a photo or a colorful card, so the color spills softly onto the page. Light Dark Add an ambient glow Give it something colorful to take its colors from. It has no color of its own. <UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:fx="https://github.com/jsuarezruiz/Nova.Avalonia.FX"> <fx:FXHost Margin="60"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:AmbientGlow /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Image Source="/Assets/album-cover.jpg" Width="200" Height="200" /> </fx:FXHost> </UserControl> Shape the light Radius sets how soft the blur is. Spread scales the colors up from the content's center, so they reach further past its edge. Saturation and Brightness make the light more or less vivid. <fx:AmbientGlow Radius="48" Spread="1.25" Saturation="1.6" Brightness="1.1" /> A larger Spread reaches further on a larger child, since it scales the content's own size. Follow content that changes The host captures the child again when its size or one of its own properties changes, such as an Image's Source. It doesn't watch the child's descendants: after changing something deeper inside, call RefreshMask() on the host. Behind a video, call it as the frames change. // PlayerHost is the FXHost around the video surface. private void OnFrameRendered(object? sender, EventArgs e) { PlayerHost.RefreshMask(); } While changes keep coming, captures are spaced about 100 ms apart, with one more once they stop. See Content masks. Properties Property Type Default Description Radius double 36 How far the colors blur, in DIPs; larger is softer and reaches further. Range 4–120. Spread double 1.12 How far the colors spread past the content, as a scale from its center. Range 1–1.6. Saturation double 1.35 How vivid the colors are: 0 gray, 1 the content's own, above 1 richer. Range 0–2.5. Brightness double 0.9 How bright the glow is: 0 none, 1 the content's own brightness. Range 0–2. Every layer also has the common properties: Intensity, Opacity, Speed, Seed, IsActive, Placement, BlendMode and RenderScale. On an ambient glow, Intensity dims the layer; Speed and Seed don't apply, since nothing moves. Notes Light and dark surfaces. On a dark surface the colors add light. On a light surface they draw as tinted haze. See Light and dark surfaces. Reduced motion. Nothing changes: the glow is still. Cost. The layer is still, so it draws when the content or a setting changes and asks for no frames in between. A redraw takes about 0.14 ms of GPU time on the bench's 340×190 card. Each capture renders the child to a bitmap on the UI thread. See Performance. Room around the host. The light reaches past the content by about 2.5 × Radius, plus what Spread adds. A clipping ancestor cuts it off: leave room around the host. Limits. Very large content is captured at a lower scale and gets a softer mask. If the child can't be captured, the host logs a warning and the layer draws nothing. See Content masks. See also AmbientGlow API reference Glow, a glow in a color you choose Pointer shadow, a shadow in the shape of the content Content masks

docs/effects/ascii.html.title: ASCII | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/effects/ascii.html.summary: ASCII ASCII art, live: the layer redraws the host's content, and anything under the host, as rows of text characters, picking for each cell the character whose ink matches the brightness there, from a blank through .-:+=%*# to @. The characters take the content's own colors, or one ink. Use it for terminal and hacker themes, a stylized picture, or a playful hover state. It goes over the child and follows whatever is drawn there, so a picture, a gradient or a video works best. Light Dark Add ASCII Put the layer over content with a range of tones, such as a picture or a gradient: <UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:fx="https://github.com/jsuarezruiz/Nova.Avalonia.FX"> <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="14"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Ascii CellSize="6" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="236" Height="128" CornerRadius="14"> <Border.Background> <LinearGradientBrush StartPoint="0%,0%" EndPoint="100%,100%"> <GradientStop Color="#7C3AED" Offset="0" /> <GradientStop Color="#EC4899" Offset="0.55" /> <GradientStop Color="#F59E0B" Offset="1" /> </LinearGradientBrush> </Border.Background> </Border> </fx:FXHost> </UserControl> Bright areas get dense characters and dark areas blanks, on a dark paper. Choose the ink and the paper By default each character takes the content's own color. Turn IsColored off to draw every character in InkColor, like a terminal. PaperColor fills the cells behind the characters; set it to Transparent to show the page instead: <fx:Ascii IsColored="False" InkColor="#4ADE80" PaperColor="#0B0D10" /> For dark ink on light paper, set IsInverted, so the darkest areas get the densest characters: <fx:Ascii IsColored="False" IsInverted="True" InkColor="#1F2937" PaperColor="#F9FAFB" /> Size the characters CellSize is the width of a character cell in DIPs; cells are 1.6 times as tall. Smaller cells show more detail. Contrast spreads the brightness, so more of the picture reaches the densest and the emptiest characters: <fx:Ascii CellSize="10" Contrast="1.6" /> Fade it in on hover Intensity fades the layer, so a transition on it turns content into text and back. This shows the picture, and turns it to ASCII while the pointer is over it: <Style Selector="fx|FXHost.ascii fx|Ascii"> <Setter Property="Intensity" Value="0" /> <Setter Property="Transitions"> <Transitions> <DoubleTransition Property="Intensity" Duration="0:0:0.3" /> </Transitions> </Setter> </Style> <Style Selector="fx|FXHost.ascii:pointerover fx|Ascii"> <Setter Property="Intensity" Value="1" /> </Style> Give the host Classes="ascii". At an Intensity of 0 the layer draws nothing and costs nothing. Properties Property Type Default Description CellSize double 7 The width of a character cell; cells are 1.6 times as tall. Range 4–24 DIPs. IsColored bool true The characters take the content's own color instead of InkColor. InkColor Color #E5E7EB The characters' color when IsColored is off. Applies when IsColored is false. PaperColor Color #0B0D10 Behind the characters; transparent shows the page. Contrast double 1.2 How far the brightness is stretched before a character is picked: above 1 pushes cells toward blank or dense, below 1 toward the middle of the ramp. Range 0.2–3. IsInverted bool false Dark areas get the densest characters (for dark ink on light paper). Every layer also has the common properties: Intensity, Opacity, Speed, Seed, IsActive, Placement, BlendMode and RenderScale. Notes Reads the backdrop: the layer copies what is drawn behind it, the child included, just before it draws, and each cell takes the average under it. Keep ancestors opaque; see Layers that read the backdrop. Needs room: on a small control the cells swallow a label. Use it on cards, panels and pictures. Still: the layer has no motion of its own; it changes only when what is behind it does. Speed and Seed don't change it, and reduced motion leaves it as it is. Light and dark surfaces: it draws the same on both; PaperColor and IsInverted set the look. Cost: 0.272 ms of GPU time per frame on a 340×190 card in the gallery's bench, plus a blurred copy of what is behind it. See Performance. The characters are small dot shapes made in the shader, not a font, so no font needs to be installed. See also Ascii API reference Dither and Halftone, which re-tone the backdrop in pixels and dots CRT, Old film and Code rain

docs/effects/aurora.html.title: Aurora | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/effects/aurora.html.summary: Aurora Northern lights inside the shape: three curtains of colored light drift slowly across it, each with a bright lower hem and fine rays, fading in from the shape's edge. Use it on hero banners, sign-in screens, empty states or a night-themed card. It draws under the host's child, as light, so it needs something dark behind it to glow against. Light Dark Add an aurora The aurora goes under the child, so a background on the child would hide it. Put the dark sky outside the host instead, and leave the child see-through: <UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:fx="https://github.com/jsuarezruiz/Nova.Avalonia.FX"> <Border CornerRadius="14" Background="#0B0F1A"> <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="14"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Aurora Feather="22" Intensity="1.6" Scale="90" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Border Width="290" Height="128" Padding="16"> <TextBlock Text="Northern lights" FontSize="17" FontWeight="Bold" Foreground="White" VerticalAlignment="Bottom" /> </Border> </fx:FXHost> </Border> </UserControl> The aurora draws the same in light and dark themes, so the same dark card works in both. Set the colors Each curtain has its own color: Color for the first, SecondColor and ThirdColor for the others. The defaults are green, blue and violet: <fx:Aurora Color="#F472B6" SecondColor="#FB923C" ThirdColor="#A78BFA" /> Shape the curtains Scale sets the size of the curtains' folds, and FlowSpeed how fast they drift; at 0 they hold still and the layer requests no more frames. Feather is how far inside the shape's edge the light fades in. Past a quarter of the shape's shorter side it counts only a quarter, so a small shape keeps a curtain rather than a thin streak: <fx:Aurora Scale="200" FlowSpeed="0.1" Feather="60" /> Fill a window The aurora's cost grows with its area. For a window-sized background, shade it at half resolution. Soft, large layers like this one are what RenderScale is for: <fx:Aurora RenderScale="0.5" /> Properties Property Type Default Description Color Color #16C79A The top curtain's color. SecondColor Color #3B6CFF The middle curtain's color. ThirdColor Color #A23BFF The bottom curtain's color. Scale double 120 Size of the curtains' folds. Range 20–400 DIPs. FlowSpeed double 0.25 How fast the curtains drift and ripple (0: still). Range 0–2 per second. Feather double 40 How far inside the shape's edge the light fades in. Past a quarter of the shorter side it counts only a quarter, so a small shape keeps a curtain rather than a thin streak. Range 0–120 DIPs. Every layer also has the common properties: Intensity, Opacity, Speed, Seed, IsActive, Placement, BlendMode and RenderScale. Notes Intensity is the strength of the light, up to 3. Seed changes the curtains' shapes. Light and dark surfaces: the aurora doesn't adapt to the surface; it is light, and it reads best over a dark background placed behind the host. For pure additive light, set BlendMode="Screen" or "Plus" (see Blend modes). Reduced motion: the curtains hold one pose. See Reduced motion. Cost: 0.127 ms of GPU time per frame on a 340×190 card in the gallery's bench. On a 700×500 panel it takes about 0.62 ms, and 0.28 ms with RenderScale="0.5". See Render scale. See also Aurora API reference Silk and Mesh gradient, calmer backgrounds Light leaks, Starfield and Fog

docs/effects/beam.html.title: Beam | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/effects/beam.html.summary: Beam Beam sends light along a curve from one point to another, over a faint track: pulses with a tail, marching dashes, or a steady shimmer. Use it to show data flowing between controls in a diagram, an integrations page, a sync screen or a pipeline. Its ends are points of the host's shape, or the centers of two controls inside the host, which it follows as the layout changes. It draws under the child, so the controls it connects sit on top of it. Light Dark Connect two controls Put the host around the panel that holds both controls, and point FromElement and ToElement at them. The beam runs between their centers, under them, and moves with them when the layout changes. <UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:fx="https://github.com/jsuarezruiz/Nova.Avalonia.FX"> <fx:FXHost> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Beam FromElement="{Binding #AppNode}" ToElement="{Binding #ApiNode}" Curvature="0.2" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Grid ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*,Auto" Width="480" Height="160"> <Border x:Name="AppNode" Grid.Column="0" Width="120" Height="72" CornerRadius="12" Background="White" BorderBrush="#E4E4E7" BorderThickness="1"> <TextBlock Text="App" FontWeight="SemiBold" Margin="14,12" /> </Border> <Border x:Name="ApiNode" Grid.Column="2" Width="120" Height="72" CornerRadius="12" Background="White" BorderBrush="#E4E4E7" BorderThickness="1"> <TextBlock Text="API" FontWeight="SemiBold" Margin="14,12" /> </Border> </Grid> </fx:FXHost> </UserControl> The controls must be inside the host. You can also set them from code: SyncBeam.FromElement = AppNode;. Without controls, From and To place the ends as shares of the shape, from 0,0 at the top left to 1,1 at the bottom right: <fx:Beam From="0.1,0.8" To="0.9,0.2" /> Styles Duration is the time a pulse, a dash or the shimmer takes to cross the path, in every style. Value Description Pulse (default) Comets with a tail, leaving every Interval seconds or on Send. Dashes Dashes marching along the path. Flow A steady shimmer running along the path. <fx:Beam Style="Dashes" DashLength="8" Duration="1.5" /> Send a pulse In the Pulse style, a pulse leaves every Interval seconds. Set Interval to 0 and call Send() to send one only when something happens, such as a request going out. PulseLength sets the tail, as a share of the path. <fx:Beam x:Name="RequestBeam" Interval="0" PulseLength="0.2" /> private void OnRequestSent(object? sender, EventArgs e) { RequestBeam.Send(); } Bow and direction Curvature bows the path to the side: 0 is straight, and at 1 the middle stands a quarter of the path's length off the straight line. Positive values bow to the left of the way the light travels (up, when it runs from left to right). IsReversed runs the light from To back to From. Color is a pulse's bright head and TailColor its tail; TrackColor and Track set the faint path under it. <fx:Beam Curvature="-0.4" IsReversed="True" Color="#34D399" TailColor="#22D3EE" Track="0.15" /> Methods Method Description Send() Sends one pulse along the path now (the Pulse style). Properties Property Type Default Description Style BeamStyle Pulse How the light travels: comets with a tail, marching dashes, or a steady shimmer. Values: Pulse, Dashes, Flow. From Point 0.08,0.5 Where the beam starts, as a share of the shape (0..1 each way). To Point 0.92,0.5 Where the beam ends, as a share of the shape (0..1 each way). Curvature double 0.25 How far the path bows to the side: 0 straight; at 1 its middle stands a quarter of its length off the straight line. Positive bows to the left of the way it travels (up, from left to right), negative the other way. Range -1 to 1. Color Color #22D3EE A pulse's bright head, and the end of the path the light runs toward. TailColor Color #A78BFA A pulse's tail, and the end of the path the light leaves from. Width double 2 Thickness of the beam's line, in DIPs; the glow around it grows with it. Range 0.5–8. Glow double 0.6 The soft light around the beam, as a share (0: none). Range 0–1 (0–100%). TrackColor Color #9CA3AF The color of the faint path under the light; its alpha scales the path along with Track. Track double 0.25 How much the path itself shows when no light is on it. Range 0–1 (0–100%). Duration double 2.5 Seconds a pulse or a dash takes to cross the path; the shimmer moves one 80-DIP wave along it in this time. Range 0.3–10. Interval double 2.5 Seconds between pulses sent on their own; 0: only those sent with Send. Range 0–10. Applies to the Pulse style. PulseLength double 0.3 A pulse's tail, as a share of the path. Range 0.05–1 (5–100%). Applies to the Pulse style. DashLength double 10 Length of a dash, in DIPs; the gaps between dashes are as long. Range 2–60. Applies to the Dashes style. IsReversed bool false Runs from To back to From. Every layer also has the common properties: Intensity, Opacity, Speed, Seed, IsActive, Placement, BlendMode and RenderScale. On a beam, Intensity dims the layer and Seed doesn't apply. Notes Light and dark surfaces. On a dark surface the light adds to what is beneath it. On a light surface it draws as tinted haze. See Light and dark surfaces. Reduced motion. The beam holds a still gradient along the path. See Reduced motion. Cost. About 0.02 ms of GPU time a frame on the bench. The layer only shades the curve and its glow, not the whole host. A Pulse beam with Interval at 0 asks for frames only while a pulse is on the path. See Performance. Many pulses. The path shows up to eight pulses at a time. With more (a short Interval), the newest are kept, so a pulse sent with Send() always shows. Several beams. Put several Beam layers in one host to draw a diagram, one per connection. See also Beam API reference Border beam, streaks running around a border Electric, lightning between two points Pulse, whose Ping style flies from one control to another One-shots and the pointer

docs/effects/beams.html.title: Beams | Nova.Avalonia.FX
docs/effects/beams.html.summary: Beams Beams paints shafts of light that drift slowly sideways over a dark background, with light falling down them: a quiet, cinematic backdrop for a hero section, a launch announcement or a dark landing page. The shafts can lean, and they're brightest at the top, where they come in. It's a fill: it paints the host's shape under the child. For light traveling along a path between two controls, see Beam instead. Light Dark Add beams Put the host around the panel, and leave the panel without a background so the beams show through it. <UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:fx="https://github.com/jsuarezruiz/Nova.Avalonia.FX"> <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="12"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Beams Count="7" Angle="12" Glow="0.7" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Grid Height="240"> <StackPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" VerticalAlignment="Center" Spacing="2"> <TextBlock Text="Launch week" Foreground="White" FontWeight="Bold" FontSize="24" HorizontalAlignment="Center" /> <TextBlock Text="Five days of new features" Foreground="#AAB4D8" FontSize="12" HorizontalAlignment="Center" /> </StackPanel> </Grid> </fx:FXHost> </UserControl> Space and lean the shafts Count is how many shafts cross the shape (12 by default). They're spaced evenly, so the count holds at any size: on a wider shape the shafts sit farther apart. Width is a shaft's average width in DIPs. A shaft is never wider than about two thirds of the space between shafts, so packed shafts stay separate, nor wider than a ninth of the shape's height, so a short shape shows streaks rather than blobs. Angle leans the shafts, in degrees from upright: positive turns them clockwise, tops to the right. Glow sets the soft light around each shaft (1 by default, 0 for none, up to 2), and Color the light's color. <fx:Beams Count="24" Width="8" Angle="-15" Glow="1.4" Color="#FDE68A" /> Each shaft drifts around its place at its own pace. Speed multiplies the clock, the drift and the falling light. Fills run on one shared clock, so beams on different hosts, with the same settings, move in step. Put the beams over your own background BackgroundColor is the color behind the beams (#06070D by default); its alpha is how opaque it is. A transparent background lets what is under the host show, such as a gradient on a border around it: <Border CornerRadius="12"> <Border.Background> <LinearGradientBrush StartPoint="0%,0%" EndPoint="0%,100%"> <GradientStop Color="#1E1B4B" Offset="0" /> <GradientStop Color="#020617" Offset="1" /> </LinearGradientBrush> </Border.Background> <fx:FXHost CornerRadius="12"> <fx:FXHost.Layers> <fx:Beams BackgroundColor="Transparent" Color="#A5B4FC" /> </fx:FXHost.Layers> <Grid Height="240" /> </fx:FXHost> </Border> The beams are added as light, so keep what is under them dark. Properties Property Type Default Description Color Color #C8D2FF The color of the shafts and of the light falling down them. BackgroundColor Color #06070D Behind the beams; transparent lets what is under the host show. Count int 12 How many shafts cross the shape. Range 1–48. Width double 14 How wide a shaft is, on average; never wider than about two thirds of the space between shafts, or a ninth of the shape's height. Range 2–80 DIPs. Glow double 1 The soft light around each shaft, a multiple: 1 is the default, 0 none. Range 0–2. Angle double 0 How far the shafts lean from upright, degrees: 0 upright; positive turns them clockwise (tops to the right). Range -60 to 60. BorderWidth double 0 Width of a band inside the edge, DIPs. 0: the whole shape. Range 0–48. UseMask bool false Paints only the child's own pixels (text, icons, a logo) instead of the shape: gradient text, a liquid-metal logo, holographic icons. It then goes over the child unless Placement says otherwise. The host captures the child to know its pixels: call RefreshMask after changing something deep inside it. Every layer also has the common properties: Intensity, Opacity, Speed, Seed, IsActive, Placement, BlendMode and RenderScale. On a fill, Intensity is its coverage, up to 1, and Seed picks each shaft's width and pace. Notes Light and dark surfaces: beams don't change with the surface. The default background is dark, so they look the same in both themes; with a transparent background, the shafts fade out over a light surface. See Light and dark surfaces. Reduced motion: the shafts and their falling light hold one fixed pose. See Reduced motion. Cost: about 0.11 ms of GPU time a frame on the benchmark's 340×190 card. Each pixel only looks at the five nearest shafts, so a higher Count doesn't cost more. The cost grows with the area. See Performance. Bands and masks: like every fill, it has BorderWidth, which paints only a band inside the edge, and UseMask, which paints only the child's own pixels, such as large text. See Content masks.
